title: Cc No. 7903 Of 2022 Kamlesh Jha vs Bijendra Jha Page 1 Of 23 on 29 July, 2026
full_text: Cc No. 7903 Of 2022 Kamlesh Jha vs Bijendra Jha Page 1 Of 23 on 29 July, 2026 DLWT020000482021 IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS-06, DISTRICT- WEST, TIS HAZARI COURTS, DELHI PRESIDED BY: SH. GAURAV SINGAL, D.J.S. Ashish Kumar Ahuja v. Great Brown Foods India Pvt. Ltd. CC NI Act No. 92-2021 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1 CNR number DLWT020000482021 2 Name of the complainant Ashish Kumar Ahuja S/o Sh. Prem Prakash Ahuja 3 Name of the accused, parentage (i) Great Brown Foods India Pvt. Ltd and residential address through its directors:- (ii) Bhuwan Mohan Gaur (iii) Chetan Gaur 4 Offence complained of or U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments proved Act, 1881 5 Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6 Final Judgment/order Acquittal 7 Date of judgment/order 29.07.2026 CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 1 of 23 Date of Institution: 06.01.2021 Date of Reserving Order: 29.07.2026 Date of Judgment: 29.07.2026 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by Ashish Kumar Ahuja (hereinafter referred to as 'the complainant') against Great Brown Foods India Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as 'the accused no. 1') through its directors, namely, Sh. Bhuwan Mohan Gaur (hereinafter referred to as 'the accused no. 2') and Sh. Chetan Gaur (hereinafter referred to as 'the accused no. 3') under section 138 read with section 142 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as 'the act'). BRIEF FACTS: 2. It is the case of the complainant that the accused no. 1 is a company, represented through its directors, i.e., the accused no. 2, Sh. Bhuwan Mohan Gaur, and the accused no. 3, Sh. Chetan Gaur. The accused nos. 1 and 2 entered into a rent agreement for the premises H-270, Sector 2, DSIIDC, Bawana, Delhi, for a period of eleven months from 28.09.2019 to 28.08.2020 for a monthly rent of Rs. 60,000 exclusive of GST, which shall be paid by the accused. 3. That the accused defaulted in making the payment of the above-mentioned liability to the complainant, and in lieu of discharging his liability, the accused, in order to discharge the legally enforceable deb,t issued the seven (07) postdated cheques. Out of which four cheques were in question. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 2 of 23 DETAILS OF THE CHEQUES IN QUESTION: Serial Cheque Cheque Date of the Cheque Date of Reasons for No. number amount cheque drawn on return memo dishonour 1. 11154 Rs. 64,800/- 05.04.2020 Axis Bank 29.06.2020 Funds Insufficient 2. 11155 Rs. 64,800/- 05.05.2020 Axis Bank 29.06.2020 Funds Insufficient 3. 11156 Rs. 64,800/- 05.06.2020 Axis Bank 29.06.2020 Funds Insufficient 4. 11157 Rs. 64,800/- 05.07.2020 Axis Bank 29.06.2020 Payment stopped by the drawer 3.1 That the complainant presented the cheque at serial 1, 2, 3 and 4 to its banker at Bank of Baroda, Branch Sansad Marg, New Delhi. The complainant, after receipt of the said dishonoured cheques, sent a legal notice dated 23.07.2020 in writing to the accused through courier, which was delivered to the address of the accused with the remark that it was "successfully delivered." The accused had failed to pay the cheque amount to the complainant within the stipulated time of 15 days. Hence. this complaint under the act is filed within the limitation period. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 3 of 23 PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COURT: 4. The file was received by way of transfer in this court. 5. After perusing the complaint and hearing the arguments of the complainant on the point of summoning of the accused, prima facie, it appeared that the offence under section 138 of the act had been made out. Hence, the cognizance of the offence was taken against the accused persons on 22.03.2021, and summons were issued to the accused persons. 6. The plea of defence of the accused no. 2 was recorded on 02.02.2022 and plea of defence of the accused no. 3 on 24.08.2022, to which the accused persons pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6.1 At this stage, the accused no. 2 admitted his signature on cheques in question but denied having filled the particulars therein. The accused stated that he didn't receive the legal demand notice, however, he admitted that his last address was correctly mentioned on the legal notice. 6.2 The accused no. 3 stated that the cheque bears the signature of accused no. 2. Accused stated that he didn't receive the legal demand notice. The cheque was issued from the company's account. He is an inactive director. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 4 of 23 7. Thereafter, considering the defence stated at the time of framing of the notice by the accused persons, this court decided to allow cross-examination of the complainant as per 145(2) of the act. During the complainant's evidence, the complainant examined himself as sole witness CW-1. The accused duly cross- examined the complainant, and the complainant's evidence was closed on 28.08.2024. 7.1 The statement of the accused persons under section 313 of the code of criminal procedure (hereinafter referred to as ' Cr.P.C .') was recorded wherein the accused no. 3 stated that he does not wish to lead defence evidence. The defence evidence on behalf of the accused no. 2 was allowed, wherein the accused no. 2 examined himself as sole witness DW-1. After which defence evidence was closed by the court on 20.08.2025. 8. On 01.07.2026, the final arguments of the parties were heard at length. EVIDENCE: 9. To prove the case, the complainant has examined himself as CW1 and has led his evidence by way of affidavit, Ex. CW1/10, and has relied upon the following documents: CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 5 of 23 Serial No. Document(s) Exhibit(s) 1. The rent agreement dated 28.09.2019 and the copy CW1/2 of ledger of the company with the certificate u/s 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. 2. Copy of reminder letters addressed to the accused CW1/3 no. 2. 3. The original cheque no. 011154, dated 05.04.2020, CW1/4 (colly.) The original cheque no. 011155, dated 05.05.2020, CW1/6 The original cheque no. 011156, dated 05.06.2020 and The original cheque no. 011157, dated 05.07.2020. 4. The original return memo dated 29.06.2020 of CW1/5 (colly.) cheque no(s) 011154, 011155, 011156 and 011157. CW1/7 5. The legal demand notice date d 23.07.2020. CW1/8 6. The courier receipts and copy of the CW1/9 and tracking/delivery report. Mark A. 10. The learned counsel for the complainant and the learned counsel for the accused orally argued at length. I have carefully perused the record, including the written submission filed on record. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 6 of 23 ARGUMENTS: 11. ARGUMENTS ON BEHALF OF THE COMPLAINANT: A) The complainant, while reiterating the contents of the complaint, has argued that all the requirements of Section 138 of the act have been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. That the accused has admitted his signature on the cheque. B) The complainant has further argued that the accused persons have not been able to raise any probable defence. Therefore, the accused persons are liable to be convicted for the offence under section 138 of the act with maximum punishment. 12. ARGUMENTS ON BEHALF OF THE ACCUSED: A) Per contra, the learned counsel for the accused, while opposing the present case, has argued that the complainant has failed to prove the essential ingredients mandated by section 138 of the act. Thus, he argued that the complaint should be dismissed and the accused be acquitted. 13. Final arguments were heard from both the parties. 13.1 I have perused the record carefully. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 7 of 23 RELEVANT PROVISIONS OF LAW: 14. Before proceeding with the present case, it would be pertinent to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides. In order to establish the offence under section 138 of the act, the complainant must fulfil all the essential ingredients of the offence. The offence under section 138 of the act is made out against the drawer of the cheque only when all the ingredients highlighted below are fulfilled beyond reasonable doubt: I. Drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AMLBC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. 14.1 Section 139 of the act provides for a presumption in favour of a holder. It reads as under: "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in section 138 , for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability." CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 8 of 23 14.2 Section 146 of the act reads as under: "The court shall, in respect of every proceedings under this chapter on production of bank's slip or memo having thereon official mark denoting that the cheque has dishonored, presume the fact of dishonor of such cheque, unless and until such fact is disproved." 14.3 Further Section 118 Clause (a) of the act provides for presumptions regarding the consideration for the Negotiable Instruments. It reads as under: "That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration". 14.4 The combined reading of the above-mentioned sections raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. However, it is a settled principle of law that the presumption under section 139 of the act can be rebutted by the accused by raising a probable defence but the burden of proof is on the accused. 15. The principles pertaining to the presumptions and the onus of proof as recently summarised by the Honorable Apex Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 as follows: "25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarize the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence. The CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 9 of 23 standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. 25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." 16. Now, it is upon the accused to displace this presumption on a scale of preponderance of probabilities and the lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt, but it need not be proved to the hilt or beyond all reasonable doubt. The accused can either prove that the liability did not exist or make the non-existence of liability so probable that a reasonable person ought, under the circumstances of the case, to act on the supposition that it does not exist. Thus, the accused can do so either by leading his own evidence in defence or even by punching holes in the case of the complainant in cross-examination. 16.1 The accused has to come forth with a convincing defence that appeals to common sense and basic rationality. Only in a case where the accused comes up with a convincing defence to counter liability can the presumption be stated to have been rebutted. Because once the execution of a cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. In the case of Kishan Rao v. Shankar Gowda, 2018 8 SCC 165, it was held that a mere denial of debt or liability cannot shift the onus CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 10 of 23 of proof from accused to complainant. All that the accused needs to establish is a probable defence. 16.2 That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 of the act imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden." It is also relevant to discuss the observation made in the case of Lekh Raj Sharma v. Yashpal Gupta (2015) 3 DLT (Cri) 521 by the Honorable High Court of Delhi as follows: "The accused is obliged to set up a probable defence. The defence cannot be only a "possible" defence. It cannot be premised on the mere ipse dixit of the accused. There should be some credible material or circumstance available on record which should lead the Court to conclude that the defence/explanation for issuance of the dishonoured cheque is a probable one." 16.3 Further, in Kishan Rao v. Shankargouda , (2018) 8 SCC 165 quoting Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513, the Honorable Apex Court held as follows: "The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should dis- prove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither permissible nor contemplated. At the same time it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of that, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumption the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 11 of 23 if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant." 17. Section 141 of the act deals with offence by companies. It states: (1)If the person committing an offence under section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any person liable to punishment if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge, or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence: Provided further that where a person is nominated as a Director of a company by virtue of his holding any office or employment in the Central Government or State Government or a financial corporation owned or controlled by the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be, he shall not be liable for prosecution under this Chapter. (2)Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where any offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. Explanation.--For the purposes of this section,-- (a)"company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and (b)"director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. 18. Section 94 of the act: The mode in which notice may be given: Notice of dishonour may be given to a duly authorized agent of the person to whom it is required to be given, or, where he has died, to his legal CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 12 of 23 representative, or, where he has been declared an insolvent, to his assignee; may be oral or written; may, if written, be sent by post; and may be in any form; but it must inform the party to whom it is given, either in express terms or by reasonable intendment that the instrument has been dishonoured, and in what way, and that he will be held liable thereon; and it must be given within a reasonable time after dishonour, at the place of business or (in case such party has no place of business) at the residence of the party for whom it is intended.If the notice is duly directed and sent by post and miscarries, such miscarriage does not render the notice invalid. APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE: 19. Coming to the present case, the accused no. 1 is a private limited company. The accused nos. 2 and 3 are its registered directors. The accused no. 3 has disputed the existence of the legal liability against him by stating that he is a inactive director in the company. The cheques in question were issued from the company's account and bear the signature of the accused no. 2. 19.1 Whereas the accused no. 2 has disputed the existence of the legal liability against him by stating that the cheques in question were given as advance cheques against the rent agreement. A security deposit of Rs. 2,00,000 to the complainant. Further, he had paid Rs. 85,500 to the electricity department for the enhancement of load, and this amount is due from the complainant. He had paid the rent for the month of February. CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 13 of 23 19.2 As far as the defence of the accused no. 3 is concerned, the Honorable Supreme Court, in Ashok Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh , 2025 INSC 427, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry , 2022 10 SCC 152, relied upon the decision in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla and others , decided on 20.09.2005, in which the Honorable court answered the reference put by the two- judge bench of the Honorable Supreme court. The Honorable court held that: (a) It is necessary to specifically aver in a complaint under Section 141 that at the time the offence was committed, the person accused was in charge of, and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. This averment is an essential requirement of Section 141 and has to be made in a complaint. Without this averment being made in a complaint, the requirements of Section 141 cannot be said to be satisfied. (b) The answer to question posed in sub-para (b) has to be in negative. Merely being a director of a company is not sufficient to make the person liable under Section 141 of the Act. A director in a company cannot be deemed to be in charge of and responsible to the company for conduct of its business. The requirement of Section 141 is that the person sought to be made liable should be in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the relevant time. This has to be averred as a fact as there is no deemed liability of a director in such cases. (c) The answer to question (c ) has to be in affirmative. The question notes that the Managing Director or Joint Managing Director would be admittedly in charge of the company and responsible to the company for conduct of its business. When that is so, holders of such positions in a company become liable under Section 141 of the Act. By virtue of the office they hold as Managing Director or Joint Managing Director, these persons are in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. Therefore, they get covered under Section 141 . So far as signatory of a cheque which is dishonoured is concerned, he is clearly responsible for the incriminating act and will be covered under sub-section (2) of Section 141 . 19.3 The Apex Court further held that "The criminal liability has been fastened on those who, at the time of the commission of the offence, were in charge of and were responsible to the firm for the conduct of the business of the firm. These may be sleeping partners CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 14 of 23 who are not required to take any part in the business of the firm; they may be ladies and others who may not know anything about the business of the firm. The primary responsibility is on the complainant to make necessary averments in the complaint so as to make the accused vicariously liable. For fastening the criminal liability, there is no presumption that every partner knows about the transaction. The obligation of the appellants to prove that at the time the offence was committed they were not in charge of and were not responsible to the firm for the conduct of the business of the firm, would arise only when first the complainant makes necessary averments in the complaint and establishes that fact. The present case is of total absence of requisite averments in the complaint." "It happens that a person may be a director in a company but he may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of the company. As a director he may be attending meetings of the Board of Directors of the Company where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. It may be that a Board of Directors may appoint sub-committees consisting of one or two directors out of the Board of the Company who may be made responsible for day-to- day functions of the Company. These are matters which form part of resolutions of Board of Directors of a Company. Nothing is oral. What emerges from this is that the role of a director in a company is a question of fact depending on the peculiar facts in each case." 19.4 In Sunita Palita (supra), it was observed: "42. ....Moreover, when a complaint is filed against a Director of the company, who is not the signatory of the dishonoured cheque, specific averments have to be made in the pleadings to substantiate the contention in the complaint, that such Director was in charge of and responsible for conduct of the business of the Company or the Company, unless such Director is the designated Managing Director or Joint Managing Director who would obviously be responsible for the company and/or its business and affairs. 19.5 Therefore, the conclusion is that the liability stems from overseeing and being accountable for the company's business operations at the relevant time when the offense occurred, rather than simply from having a title or position within the company. Liability is determined by the individual's role in a company's operations rather than their title or position. The liability originates from the actions, behaviors, or failures of an individual and is not solely due to occupying CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 15 of 23 a role or position within a company. Responsibility is assigned to individuals who might be associated with the disputed transaction. Consequently, to establish a case under section 141 of the act, the complaint must reveal the essential facts that render an individual liable. 19.6 After perusing Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/10 it appears that the specific allegations exist against the accused nos. 1, 2 and 3. Reference drawn to paragraph nos. 7, 13, 14 and 15 of Ex. CW1/1 and to paragraphs nos.14, and 15 of Ex. CW1/10. The court is of the view, after taking into consideration the jurisprudence and the above discussion, that specific averments against accused nos. 1, 2, and 3 were made by the complainant, which prima facie shows that at the relevant time the accused no. 1 was represented by the accused nos. 2 and 3. His mere statement that he is not an active member is not sufficient to absolve him from his liability as a director. The onus is on him to prove his status as a 'inactive director.' 20. The complainant has relied upon Ex. CW1/2, Ex. CW1/3, Ex. CW1/4 (colly.), Ex. CW1/5 (colly.), CW1/6, CW1/7, CW1/8, CW1/9, and Mark A. The cross-examination of the complainant was closed vide the order dated 28.08.2024. 21. It is established that the said cheques in question, Ex. CW1/4 (colly.) and Ex. CW1/6, were signed by the accused no. 2 in the capacity of the director of the company. They were presented to the bank within three months, and the same were returned due to "funds insufficient" and "payment stopped by the drawer" vide Ex. CW1/5 (colly.) and Ex. CW-1/7 respectively. The ingredient qua the demand of the aforesaid cheque amount within 30 days of receipt of information CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 16 of 23 of its dishonor has also been proved vide. CW1/8, CW1/9 (colly.) and Mark A, which is the legal notice dated 23.07.2020 along with the courier receipt and its tracking report. However, the tracking report was not accompanied with the mandatory certificate under section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 . The admissibility of electronic evidence necessitates compliance with the above- mentioned certificate, which has not been met in this instance. Consequently, the documentation submitted by the complainant regarding this aspect is inadmissible as evidence. Reliance is placed on Arjun Panditrao Khotkar vs Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal , AIR 2020 Supreme Court 490. Consequently, the service of the legal notice by the complainant to the accused has not been proved as per the law. 21.1 The learned counsel for the accused persons submit that the accused persons never received the legal demand notice. Hence, the present matter is liable to be dismissed, as the complainant has failed to prove the ingredient of service. 21.2 The learned counsel for the complainant submits that the addressee, as per the courier receipts, Ex. CW1/9, of the legal notice, are the accused persons, i.e., 1, 2 and 3. The tracking report, Mark A, reflects that the courier was delivered to the addressee. The accused no. 2 states that the legal demand notice bears the correct address. Therefore, it can be presumed that element of service exists in favour of the complainant. 21.3 The issue at hand is whether a written notice sent by courier is deemed valid under Section 138 of the act in the absence of a certificate as per Section CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 17 of 23 65B of the IEA, and whether the presumption of service outlined in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act pertains to this method of service. 21.4 An integrated understanding of Section 138 and Section 94 of the act suggests that the notice for cheque dishonor should be in written form, and if it is written, it can be sent by post to utilize the benefits outlined in the latter portion of Section 94 of the act. If it is correctly addressed, then even in the case of a miscarriage, the notice will still be deemed valid. Therefore, although section 94 of the act permits the written notice to be dispatched by mail, it does not mandate that it must be sent through postal services. The expression "may, if documented, be dispatched by mail" holds particular importance. 21.5 In Section 94 of the act, the word "may" concerning the sending of the written notice by post is permissive and not mandatory. As a result, sending the written notice through a courier service is not restricted by section 94 of the act. The only advantage of sending the notice by mail is explained in the latter section 94 of the act; this indicates that if the notice is sent to the proper address, it will remain valid, even if it doesn't reach the intended destination. The phrase "service through post" is outlined in section 27 of the General Clauses Act, indicating that for the presumption of notice service to apply, it must be sent using registered post. Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, states that: 27. Meaning of service by post.--Where any 2[Central Act] or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre- paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 18 of 23 and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. 21.6 Section 27 of the General Clauses Act outlines the postal service, which provides only registered mail. Speed posts are considered registered mail as well. Nevertheless, from the earlier analysis, it is clear that courier services are included under section 94 of the act; however, to take advantage of section 27 of the General Clauses Act, a notice must be dispatched by registered mail, and courier services do not qualify as registered mail. As a result, until the amendment under section 27 of the General Clauses Act is enacted to include courier service alongside registered post, the presumption of service for registered post under section 27 of the General Clauses Act does not apply to notices sent through courier service. As a result, the assumption of service delivery of notice under section 27 of the General Clauses Act is applicable only when the notice is sent via registered mail, rather than through a courier service. Therefore, to ensure valid delivery of the legal notice via courier, the complainant needs to present the tracking report along with the certificate under section 65B of the IEA. 21.7 On this, the Honorable Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed and another , Appeal (crl.) 767 of 2007, has stated that 14. Section 27 gives rise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post. In view of the said presumption, when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that in spite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice. Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been effected at the time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business. This Court has already CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 19 of 23 held that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement, due service has to be presumed.It is, therefore, manifest that in view of the presumption available under Section 27 of the Act, it is not necessary to aver in the complaint under Section 138 of the Act that service of notice was evaded by the accused or that the accused had a role to play in the return of the notice unserved. 21.8 The court cited Section 114 of the IEA, specifically Illustration (f), to demonstrate that there is no "material difference" between Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the IEA. Taking into account the situation and deficiencies in the existing case, the mentioned presumption is not applicable. Section 114 and the related illustration are presented below: "114. Court may presume existence of certain facts. - The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case. Illustrations But the Court shall also have regard to such facts as the following, in considering whether such maxims do or do not apply to the particular case before it: -- as to illustration (f) -- the question is, whether a letter was received. It is shown to have been posted, but the usual course of the post was interrupted by disturbances;" 22. It is trite that the procedure is handmaid to justice. Its purpose is to serve justice. Such cannot be allowed to come in the way of justice. Now, the question arises: at what stage should the production of the mandatory certificate be allowed? CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 20 of 23 22.1 The Honorable Supreme Court has answered the same in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (supra). It was held that Depending on the facts of each case, and the Court exercising discretion after seeing that the accused is not prejudiced by want of a fair trial, the Court may in appropriate cases allow the prosecution to produce such certificate at a later point in time. If it is the accused who desires to produce the requisite certificate as part of his defence, this again will depend upon the justice of the case - discretion to be exercised by the Court in accordance with law. 22.2 The learned counsel for the complainant, during the final arguments, requested approval to present the certificate as per section 65B of the IEA. Considering the above, the court is of the view that this case was initiated in 2021 and set for final arguments/judgment since 03.09.2025. The complainant had sufficient chances to confirm the gap. It was only after the court raised the issue of the certificate not being tendered that the complainant learned of the gap. Allowing the present application would essentially amount to filling of the void left by the complainant in the case, which would unfairly disadvantage the accused. 23. Taking into account the aforementioned facts and circumstances of the present case and without going into the veracity of the testimony of DW1, the court is of the view that in order to pronouce a conviction in a criminal case, the guilt of the accused should not be based on mere surmises and conjectures but it should be based on cogent evidence. The prosecution must stand on its own. In the present case, the complainant has failed to establish the crucial element of section 138 of the act, i.e., the delivery of the legal demand notice, and the accused has successfully contradicted the presumption of a legally enforceable debt CC No. 7903 of 2022 Kamlesh Jha Versus Bijendra Jha Page 21 of 23 concerning the amount of the cheque involved. Subsequently, the responsibility to establish the elements of the offence under Section 138 of the NI Act against the accused beyond reasonable doubt reverted to the complainant. The complainant has failed to discharge the said onus as contemplated under section 138 of the act. 24. Considering the discussion above, due to the inability of the complainant to prove the elements of the offense under Section 138 of the act against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused persons namely (i) Great Brown Foods India Pvt. Ltd and its directors (ii) Bhuwan Mohan Gaur (iii) Chetan Gaur are hereby acquitted of the offense under Section 138 NI Act. 25. Previous bail bonds/personal bonds of the accused person(s) stand canceled. 26. Bonds under Section 437 A Cr.P.C. have been furnished. The same are hereby accepted for a period of six months from today.
